Level 3 · Advanced · Week 8

Data Detectives

Data tells stories when you clean it, count it and chart it.

What you will learn

  • How to read a CSV file with Python’s csv module.
  • How to clean messy data: extra spaces, MiXeD capitals, empty rows, missing numbers.
  • How to count with a dictionary and work out an average.
  • How to draw a bar chart that everyone can read – and how to keep survey answers private.

The big idea: the data detective’s pipeline

A data detective always works in the same order. Skipping a step gives wrong answers!

1. Read: what is a CSV file?

CSV means comma-separated values: a table saved as plain text. The first line is the header (the column names). Every other line is one row. Here is the start of favorite_games.csv – made-up, anonymous survey answers (a response number, no names):

response,age_group,favorite_game,genre,hours_per_week,stars
1,10-11,Block Craft,building,5,5
2,12-13, block craft ,building,3,4
5,,,,,
7,12-13,Kart Dash,racing,,3

csv.DictReader turns each row into a dictionary: row["favorite_game"] is "Block Craft".

import csv
with open("favorite_games.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        print(row["favorite_game"], row["stars"])

2. Clean: wash the data first

Every value arrives as text, even numbers: "5", not 5. And people type things in different ways. Spot the mess:

Messy value Problem Clean it with
" block craft " extra spaces, small letters .strip().title() → "Block Craft"
"BLOCK CRAFT" capitals .title() → "Block Craft"
"5" a number stored as text int("5") → 5
"" (hours) missing answer use None, and skip it in averages
5,,,,, empty row skip the whole row

3 and 4. Count and calculate

Counting with a dictionary is like a tally chart. The first time you see a game, counts.get(game, 0) gives 0:

counts = {}
for row in rows:
    game = row["favorite_game"]
    counts[game] = counts.get(game, 0) + 1
# {"Block Craft": 5, "Kart Dash": 4, ...}

The average (mean) is the total divided by how many: sum(numbers) / len(numbers). Leave out missing answers – counting a blank as 0 would make the average unfairly small.

5. Chart: readable by everyone

A good chart never relies on color alone. Write the name under each bar and the number on top, so someone who sees colors differently can still read it.

Exercise8.1: Survey cleaner

Folder: week08/ex-survey-cleaner. Open favorite_games.csv in Thonny and circle the mess you find. Then finish to_number(), is_empty() and add .title() to the game names. Done: Clean answers: 17.

How many rows did the cleaner throw away, and why?

Exercise8.2: Survey stats

Folder: week08/ex-survey-stats. Finish count_by(), average() and most_popular(). Then answer from your program’s report:

Most popular game: (blank to fill in) Average hours per week: (blank to fill in)

Adventure games got 5.0 stars on average from only 2 answers. Should we trust that? Why?

Exercise8.3: Bar chart

Folder: week08/ex-bar-chart. Make bar_height() scale the bars so the biggest is MAX_HEIGHT pixels, and write a number on top and a name under every bar. Done: six labeled bars from Block Craft (5) to Space Chess (1).

SafetyConsent and privacy in surveys

Before collecting data, ask: Did people agree to answer? Can they skip a question? Do I really need this question? Never collect real names, addresses, schools, birthdays or photos. Even without names, answers together can point to one person (“the only 13-year-old in the chess club”). Before sharing data, anonymize it: keep only the columns you need and give each row an ID like R1, R2.

Reflect

What story does the bar chart tell? What can it not tell us?

Would you answer a survey that asked for your full name? Why or why not?

New words

CSV
Comma-separated values: a table saved as plain text, one row per line.
header
The first line of a CSV file, with the column names.
data cleaning
Fixing messy data (spaces, capitals, missing or empty values) before using it.
average (mean)
The total divided by how many values there are.
sample
The group of people who answered. A small sample can give misleading results.
consent
Agreeing, freely, to take part – with the choice to say no.
anonymize
Remove or replace anything that could show who gave an answer.

Homework: Data Detectives

15–20 minutes. Do Core first; Challenge and Creative are optional.

CoreAnonymize a survey (about 10 minutes)

Open 3-advanced/exercises/week08/hw-survey-privacy/starter.py and press F5. The file snack_survey.csv is made up, but it has a nickname and a club column. Together they could show exactly who answered.

  1. Finish anonymize(rows, keep): each new row gets an id (R1, R2, ...) and only the columns in keep.

  2. Run again. The first row should be {’id’: ’R1’, ’favorite_snack’: ’apple slices’, ’minutes_reading’: ’20’}.

Why is club risky even without a name?

ChallengeSave the safe file

Finish save_csv(rows, filename) with csv.DictWriter: open the file with "w" and newline="", write the header, then the rows. Run the program and open snack_survey_anonymous.csv in Thonny (File → Open, choose “All files”). Which snack is the most popular? (blank to fill in)

CreativeDesign a kind, safe survey

Plan a 4-question survey for your family about a fun topic (favorite board game, best pizza topping, dream pet). Rules: start with a consent sentence (“You can skip any question”); no names, ages, addresses or schools; at least one question with a number answer you could average.

Self-checkSelf-check: tick each box when it is true
